newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican companies in battle over prized railway.
newsitem.headline: Mexican companies in battle over prized railway.

text.p: A decision due Thursday on bidding for Mexico's Northeast Railway could also determine the nation's transportation king, analysts say.

The government is scheduled to reveal the winning bid for the nation's most important railway, which links the capital with the U.S. border and key shipping ports. U.S. analysts have estimated the route's worth at $600 million.
Facing off in the bidding are reigning transport leader Transportacion Maritima Mexicana (TMM) and construction giant Empresas ICA.
Analysts say a third bid by Grupo Mexico lacks the foreign support to compete with the other two powerhouses.

TMM has teamed up with Kansas City Southern Industries Inc in its bid and also owns a railroad from Mexico's border that links Texas to Chicago. In addition, the company jointly operates the northern part of a bridge crossing the U.S.-Mexico border through Nuevo Laredo, Tamaulipas and Laredo, Texas. "We see a lot of potential for growth. Unlike a lot of other railroads in Latin America, this is more like an extension of a U.S. railroad," Joe Monello, chief financial operator of Kansas City Southern, told Reuters.

TMM already operates ports in Manzanillo, Colima state and Tuxpan, Tamaulipas state, and also has trucking interests and international holdings, which keep the company's assets diversified, said Phokion Potamianos, senior oil and shipping analyst with Caspian Securities in New York.

"The growing trend with shipping companies is providing water and land-based transport. There is a greater premium if you can guarantee transport, say from Japan to Mexico, that is traceable, secure and accountable," he said.
On the other hand, ICA has no current railroad interests, but control over the Northeast Railway could launch the company to lead the nation in transportation, analysts say.
"If ICA wins the railroad concession, it will become leader in transportation, and it will fit very well with its operations," Claudia Gonzalez, construction analyst with Abaco brokerage, said.
Northeast Railway tracks link the capital and U.S. border with the nation's largest shipping port in Veracruz, where ICA recently won the government operating concession.
The railroad would also complement ICA's diversification plans, adding to its holdings in ports, bridges and freeways.
ICA has said it would do any necessary improvements on the line, and that its partner Union Pacific Corp would provide the "know-how" for the railway's operations.
The Northeast line carries 60 percent of Mexico's grain imports and 90 percent of vehicle and autoparts imports, and is considered the jewel of the country's railway system.
"The market is especially focused on the Northeast because it was inefficiently run and was not used to its potential," Potamianos said.

Despite the neck-to-neck battle for the railroads, analysts predict the competitors may decide to share haulage rights, allowing one another equal access across the routes without extra fees. "I would be surprised if the government did not allow cooperation because of all the synergies to be gained," Potamianos said.

Competition for the Northeast railway has dwindled to three, after the Communications and Transport ministry confirmed two foreign companies were unlikely to be considered because they do not fill the minimum national ownership requirements.

Although not formally excluded, ministry officials said Illinois Central Corp and the consortium led by French company GEC-Alsthom NV ALSF.CN are not 51 percent owned by a Mexican company, as privatization law requires.
